sources.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
sources.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon, Mert Demirer
sources.locator: PDF pp. 3–5, Study Design/Results; pp. 7–8, discussion/limitations
sources.claim: 95 professional programmers recruited and randomized; among task completers, mean completion time 71.17 minutes with Copilot versus 160.89 without, a 55.8% reduction in a standardized JavaScript HTTP-server task.
sources.qualification: Authors report 35 completers in each group. Completion is based on passing 12 tests, not a comprehensive maintainability/security assessment. Narrow task, older tool and nonrepresentative recruitment; paper explicitly leaves code-quality effects unexamined. Microsoft/GitHub affiliations are disclosed on p. 1.
sources.direction: Supports useful code-generation assistance; opposes extrapolating a narrow result into universal productivity, autonomy or a 10x criterion.
sources.method: Randomized controlled experiment; outcome conditional on completing the task.
sources.numbers: 1 - 71.17/160.89 = 0.557648 (~55.8% less time); 160.89/71.17 = 2.26064 times the task throughput if quality/task assumptions hold, not 10x. The speed-ratio interpretation is analyst arithmetic, not an independently measured population effect.
sources.verification: Original full paper or issuer report retrieved over verified HTTPS; relevant methods, results and limitations inspected. Findings below are source claims, not independently replicated results.

sources.title: Generative AI at Work
sources.authors: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, Lindsey R. Raymond
sources.locator: PDF abstract p. 2; data p. 13; empirical strategy p. 15; conclusion PDF pp. 29–30 (printed pp. 27–28)
sources.claim: Study of 5,179 customer-support agents reports 14% higher issues resolved per hour on average, with larger gains for novice/lower-skilled workers, from staggered introduction of a generative-AI assistant.
sources.qualification: Observational staggered rollout with difference-in-differences, not a randomized trial; one business setting and human agents remain in the workflow. Does not establish long-run labor-market outcomes or generalize to every firm. The NBER page points to a 2025 QJE publication, but this dossier verifies and cites the November-2023 working-paper version, not uninspected final-version estimates.
sources.direction: Supports usefulness beyond coding and possible diffusion of expertise; does not prove multi-tier categorical dissolution or measured society-wide democratization.
sources.method: Field evidence; difference-in-differences and identifying assumptions.
sources.numbers: 14% higher issues/hour corresponds to 1.14 times that metric, not 10 times. Do not treat it as a time reduction or combine it numerically with S1.

sources.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
sources.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Beth Barnes, David Rein (METR)
sources.publication_date: 2025-07-10 organizational report; retrieved arXiv paper v2 dated 2025-07-25
sources.locator: PDF abstract and §§2–3; original report Core Result/Methodology and its 2026 update warning
sources.claim: 16 experienced open-source developers completed 246 tasks with randomized AI access; early-2025 tools increased implementation time by 19% in that setting.
sources.qualification: Specific developers, mature familiar repositories and February–June 2025 tools, chiefly Cursor and Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet. Not a claim about all developers or current tools. The original METR web page explicitly says the historical result is out of date; read S4 and S5 with it.
sources.direction: Opposes universal acceleration and equating perceived gains with measured gains; does not establish that LLMs lack useful capability.
sources.method: Task-level randomized controlled trial, realistic repository work.
sources.numbers: 19% longer time means 1.19 times completion time, not 19% less throughput; inverse throughput would be ~0.8403 under identical-task assumptions. Do not compare its time outcome directly to S2 issues/hour.

sources.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
sources.authors: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein, Khalid Mahamud (METR)
sources.locator: Opening summary; Wider adoption of AI has made it more difficult to measure task-level productivity; Details of the productivity study
sources.claim: METR reports that later-2025 follow-up data gives an unreliable signal of current productivity because participant/task selection and concurrent-agent time measurement undermine interpretation. Authors believe acceleration likely increased, but call their data very weak evidence for its size.
sources.qualification: Original follow-up report, not proof of a precise current causal gain. Developer reluctance to work without AI is selection evidence, not proof civilization cannot function without LLMs. Do not use the old 19% slowdown as a current estimate or the follow-up as a verified large gain.
sources.direction: Supports the possibility of increased usefulness and changed workflows; opposes confident current magnitudes and overclaiming suppression-test irreversibility.
sources.method: Follow-up experiment with acknowledged recruitment, task-selection, pay-rate, quality and time-measurement problems.
sources.numbers: No follow-up point estimate is used in the snapshot because the issuer calls the signal unreliable.

sources.title: Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity
sources.locator: Summary; Methodology; Results/Productivity gains around March 2026; Qualitative impressions
sources.claim: Survey of 349 technical workers reports median self-reported value multipliers between 1.4x and 2x across three measures; median self-reported speed multiplier is 3x.
sources.qualification: Convenience sample, low email response rates, self-reported counterfactuals and possible overstatement; value and speed differ. The authors explicitly warn that internal consistency does not establish reality and are skeptical of especially high estimates. Not causal measured productivity, general-population evidence or demonstrated 10x impact.
sources.direction: Current positive reports supporting perceived usefulness, balanced against measurement and selection weaknesses; not an independent confirmation of S3/S4.
sources.method: Original survey, not experiment; shares issuer with S3/S4.
sources.numbers: Retain the distinctions among 1.4–2x self-reported value, 3x self-reported speed and actual measured effects. No metric reaches a verified general 10x conclusion here.

sources.title: Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI
sources.authors: Tao Tu, Anil Palepu, Mike Schaekermann, et al. (Google Research / Google DeepMind)
sources.locator: PDF abstract p. 1; study design/results; Discussion pp. 17–20
sources.claim: Specialized LLM-based AMIE was compared with 20 primary-care physicians across 149 simulated scenarios in a randomized double-blind crossover study of text consultations. Authors report higher diagnostic accuracy and better performance on many rated axes in that evaluation.
sources.qualification: Patient actors, text-only interface unfamiliar to clinicians, specialized system and limited representativeness/blinding; not a live-patient safety trial or an evaluation of clinical-documentation benefits. It does not prove that generic deployable LLM systems inherit AMIE performance. Authors require further research before real-world translation.
sources.direction: Supports the plausibility of capabilities beyond code/customer support; opposes attributing specialized simulated performance to generic LLM systems or authorizing hospital deployment.
sources.method: Original experimental preprint, simulated clinical consultations, not routine clinical outcomes.
sources.numbers: Use the verified 149 scenarios/20 physicians only for study scope, not effect magnitude or tenfold claims. No clinical outcome reduction is inferred.

sources.title: Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants?
sources.authors: Neil Perry, Megha Srivastava, Deepak Kumar, Dan Boneh
sources.publication_date: 2022-11-07 initial preprint; 2023 CCS conference paper; retrieved arXiv v3 dated 2023-12-18
sources.locator: PDF abstract/introduction p. 1; §3 study design and Table 1; §4 security results; §7.2 limitations
sources.claim: In a 47-participant study of five analyzed security-related programming tasks, participants with an AI assistant generally wrote less secure code and were more likely to believe their code was secure; insecure solutions occurred more often for four of five tasks.
sources.qualification: Assistant based on codex-davinci-002, small mostly-student sample, security-task setting and older system. No current incidence or universal risk rate can be inferred. Not a reason to deny all productivity benefits; correctness and security need separate measurement.
sources.direction: Opposes treating code generation as reliable autonomous delivery and supports retaining oversight/security validation.
sources.method: Randomized user study with unequal group sizes; manually assessed correctness/security.
sources.numbers: Do not invent a pooled vulnerability percentage or claim significance for every task; retain task heterogeneity.
